stance_labels.null-or-contrary: Null, or points to other explanations
stance_labels.critical-commentary: Critical of the term or the claims
stance_labels.supports-association: Reports or argues for a link
stance_labels.neutral-background: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)

note: All entries are secondary-only as of this date. Nothing may be published until each source is read (abstract at minimum).

rows.title: Montes (2016): screen time in autistic and non-autistic US children aged 6 to 17
rows.short_title: Montes 2016: screen time in US school-age autistic children
rows.stance_label: Null, or points to other explanations
rows.one_line: In a US national survey, autistic and non-autistic children aged 6 to 17 had similar total screen time.

rows.title: Ophir et al. (2023): a systematic review and meta-analysis of screen time and autism
rows.short_title: Ophir 2023: meta-analysis of screen time and autism
rows.stance_label: Null, or points to other explanations
rows.one_line: 46 studies: a positive pooled link that became much smaller and non-significant after correction for publication bias.

rows.title: Takahashi N et al. (2023): genetic likelihood of autism and screen time in toddlers
rows.short_title: Takahashi N 2023: autism genetics and toddler screen time
rows.type: Cohort with polygenic risk scores (Hamamatsu Birth Cohort)
rows.stance_label: Null, or points to other explanations
rows.one_line: Children with higher genetic likelihood of autism spent more time on screens from toddlerhood, pointing to reverse causation or shared causes.

rows.title: Zhang et al. (2023): shared genetic risk in the link between screen time and children's psychiatric problems
rows.short_title: Zhang 2023: shared genetics, screen time and outcomes
rows.stance_label: Null, or points to other explanations
rows.one_line: Shared genetic risk explained much of the screen-time link with attention problems in 9-to-11-year-olds.

rows.title: Cai et al. (2025): a Mendelian randomization study of leisure screen time and six neurodevelopmental conditions
rows.short_title: Cai 2025: Mendelian randomization finds no causal ASD signal
rows.stance_label: Null, or points to other explanations
rows.one_line: No evidence that genetically predicted leisure screen time affects autism; the genetic proxies reflect adult habits, not infant exposure.

rows.title: Early screen time and behavior trajectories in autistic, ADHD and other children (Australia, 2026)
rows.short_title: Australia 2026: early screens and emotional trajectories
rows.stance_label: Null, or points to other explanations
rows.one_line: More early screen time went with a small rise in emotional-problem scores in all groups, with no extra effect in autistic or ADHD children.

rows.title: French critique: "the viral alert without scientific foundation" (c. 2017-2018)
rows.short_title: French critique: 'screens and autism' alert lacked basis
rows.type: Critical commentary (online forum post; grey literature)
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: Argued that the 2017 French alert linking screens and autism had no scientific basis.

rows.title: Alper (2020): a letter on improving research about screens, autism and families
rows.short_title: Alper 2020: letter on improving screens-autism research
rows.type: Published letter, with the original authors' reply
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: A media and disability researcher's letter calling for better research on screens, autism and families; the authors replied.

rows.title: Science Media Centre (2020): expert reaction to the infant screen-time study
rows.short_title: UK experts react to the 2020 infant screen-time study
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: Independent UK researchers said the 2020 study's screen measure was crude, it diagnosed no one, and it did not look at context.

rows.title: Lin, Lin and Gau (2022): "Screen timing may be more likely than screen time"
rows.short_title: Lin YH 2022 letter: screen timing vs. total screen time
rows.type: Published letter, with the original authors' reply
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: Argued that when screens are used, especially before sleep, may matter more than total screen time.

rows.title: Detroja and Bhatia (2024): "the trepidations of virtual autism"
rows.short_title: Detroja & Bhatia 2024: too early to call it a diagnosis
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: Concludes the evidence is too preliminary for a diagnosis, and stresses that screens and early autistic traits may influence each other.

rows.title: Krijnen et al. (2026): "Why the term 'virtual autism' warrants caution"
rows.short_title: Krijnen et al. 2026: why 'virtual autism' warrants caution
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: Argues the word 'autism' here revives parent blame, misrepresents autism and suggests screens cause it; proposes 'screen-related developmental delay'.

rows.title: van Asselt (2026): "Beyond screen time", a neurodiversity-affirming research agenda
rows.short_title: van Asselt 2026: a neurodiversity-affirming research agenda
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: Argues screen research on autism is risk-focused and deficit-based, and proposes six principles centred on how and why media are used.

rows.title: Dhungel, Pokhrel and Karki (2026): "Screen-induced developmental deviation is not autism"
rows.short_title: Dhungel et al. 2026: 'neither virtual nor autism'
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: Argues the picture is 'neither virtual nor autism', the label adds stigma, and proposes a research term that itself assumes causation.

rows.title: Romanian critique: "Adevărul despre autismul virtual" (The truth about virtual autism)
rows.short_title: Romanian critique: 'The truth about virtual autism'
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: Argues the only 'study' behind the term is an essay that lacks scientific rigor and was not published in a recognized scientific journal.

rows.title: autismus Deutschland: position statement on "virtueller Autismus"
rows.short_title: German autism association on 'virtueller Autismus'
rows.type: Position statement from a national autism association
rows.stance_label: Critical of the term or the claims
rows.one_line: Says the term is not a recognized medical term and warns that linking autism to screens revives the false idea that autism comes from parenting.

rows.title: Slobodin, Heffler and Davidovitch (2019): a systematic review of screen media and autism
rows.short_title: Slobodin 2019: systematic review of screen media and autism
rows.stance_label: Mixed or conditional findings
rows.one_line: Autistic children and teens use screens more and start younger; content and context may matter; effects of exposure before 3 were largely unexamined.

rows.title: Heffler et al. (2020): early screen viewing, parent-child play and autism-like checklist scores
rows.short_title: Heffler 2020: infant screens, play and autism checklists
rows.type: Cohort (secondary analysis of the US National Children's Study)
rows.stance_label: Mixed or conditional findings
rows.one_line: TV/video at 12 months had a small link to higher autism-checklist scores at age 2 but not to screening 'at risk'; daily play went with lower scores.

rows.title: Hill et al. (2020): screen time at 36 months in children with and without a family history of autism or ADHD
rows.short_title: Hill et al. 2020: screen time at 36 months
rows.type: Cross-sectional analysis within a familial-likelihood cohort
rows.stance_label: Mixed or conditional findings
rows.one_line: Three-year-olds with ADHD concerns watched more; more screen time went with lower language; the autism-group result is unconfirmed.

rows.title: Dong et al. (2021): screen time among 193 autistic preschoolers in China
rows.short_title: Dong et al. 2021: screen time among autistic preschoolers
rows.stance_label: Mixed or conditional findings
rows.one_line: Autistic preschoolers averaged 2.6 h/day; only 34% had screen time with a parent who talked with them; correlations were weak.

rows.title: Melchior et al. (2022): screen use and autism screening at age 2 in the French ELFE cohort
rows.short_title: Melchior 2022: screens at 2 and autism screening (France)
rows.type: Cohort (cross-sectional analysis within a national birth cohort)
rows.stance_label: Mixed or conditional findings
rows.one_line: Screen use at 2 had a very small link to medium autism-screening scores but a lower chance of high-risk scores: no simple pattern.

rows.title: Sarfraz et al. (2023): a systematic review of early screen time and autism
rows.short_title: Sarfraz 2023: mixed evidence on early screens and autism
rows.stance_label: Mixed or conditional findings
rows.one_line: Found mixed evidence and concluded there were not enough data to confirm any link between early screen time and autism.

rows.title: Lin, Wu and Guo (2025): screen time before age 2 and autism by age 12
rows.short_title: Lin et al. 2025: screens at 2 and autism at 12 (Australia)
rows.type: Research letter; cohort with conventional and instrumental-variable analyses
rows.stance_label: Mixed or conditional findings
rows.one_line: Heavy screen time at 2 was linked to autism by 12 in a standard analysis, but not in an instrumental-variable analysis.

rows.title: Tbilisi, Georgia (2025): does the timing or amount of early screen time relate to autism screening scores?
rows.short_title: Georgia 2025: timing of first screens and M-CHAT-R scores
rows.type: Cross-sectional in practice (described by the authors as an observational cohort)
rows.stance_label: Mixed or conditional findings
rows.one_line: High-risk screens were about 3 times as common with first exposure before 6 months; daily duration explained about 2% of score variation.

rows.title: Ozyazici (2026): "Examining the concept of virtual autism"
rows.short_title: Ozyazici 2026: examining the 'virtual autism' concept
rows.stance_label: Mixed or conditional findings
rows.one_line: Says the concept is not a diagnosis and names key gaps (no long-term studies, no randomized trials), but its advice uses causal-sounding language.

rows.title: Waldman et al. (2008): rainfall, autism rates and the early "TV" idea
rows.short_title: Waldman 2008: rain, TV and autism rates (a history note)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Counties with more rain had higher autism rates; the authors speculated about indoor TV time. No child-level screen data.

rows.title: Chonchaiya, Nuntnarumit and Pruksananonda (2011): television viewing in autistic toddlers and controls
rows.short_title: Chonchaiya 2011: TV viewing in autistic and other toddlers
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Autistic Thai toddlers had watched about 3 times as much TV and started about 6 months earlier than controls.

rows.title: Dunckley: "Electronic Screen Syndrome" (popular book, 2015, and book chapter)
rows.short_title: Dunckley: 'Electronic Screen Syndrome' (book and chapter)
rows.type: Popular book and book chapter (clinical opinion)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Coined 'Electronic Screen Syndrome', a proposed disorder of mood, attention and arousal; no controlled studies; not a recognized diagnosis.

rows.title: Heffler and Oestreicher (2016): an untested model of screens and social brain development
rows.short_title: Heffler & Oestreicher 2016: an untested brain model
rows.type: Hypothesis paper (theoretical model, no new data)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Proposed that heavy early audiovisual stimulation might strengthen non-social brain pathways at the expense of social ones in some infants. Untested.

rows.title: "Écrans et autisme" (France, 2017): a continuing-education handout
rows.short_title: 'Écrans et autisme' (France, 2017): a clinician handout
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Part of France's 2017 public alarm that heavy tablet and phone use might produce an autism-like picture in toddlers. Anecdotal.

rows.title: Zamfir (2018): the paper that coined "autism virtual"
rows.short_title: Zamfir 2018: where the term 'virtual autism' began
rows.type: Retrospective review of clinic case histories, with an uncontrolled group comparison
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Coined the term. Looked back at Romanian children already diagnosed with autism and reported that many had heavy early screen use, by parent recall.

rows.title: Zamfir's Romanian essays and dissertation on "autismul virtual" (2018)
rows.short_title: Zamfir's Romanian essays on 'autismul virtual'
rows.type: Essays and a master's dissertation (grey literature, not peer reviewed)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Romanian essays restating the idea, with anecdotes of quick change after screens stopped. No comparison group.

rows.title: Marcelli, Bossière and Ducanda (2018): a proposed syndrome called EPEE
rows.short_title: Marcelli et al. 2018: the proposed 'EPEE' syndrome
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: French clinicians proposed 'EPEE', a set of signs in heavily screen-exposed toddlers, and deliberately avoided the word autism.

rows.title: Hermawati et al. (2018): a small case series from Indonesia
rows.short_title: Hermawati 2018: a small Indonesian case series
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: A few young children with heavy early screen use all had speech delay and short attention; no comparison group.

rows.title: Harlé (2019): the hypothesis paper that proposed "virtual autism"
rows.short_title: Harlé 2019: the 'virtual autism' hypothesis paper
rows.type: Hypothesis paper and narrative review (no new data)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Argued that intensive early screen exposure might play a part in autism-like signs in some young children, and proposed the label. A hypothesis, not a test.

rows.title: Devenir (2020): EPEE described as a new syndrome
rows.short_title: Devenir 2020: EPEE described as a new syndrome
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Develops the EPEE proposal with the same set of signs and the same claim that they lessen after screens stop. No controls.

rows.title: Chen et al. (2020): do caregiver interaction, sleep or outdoor play explain the screen link?
rows.short_title: Chen et al. 2020: interaction, sleep and outdoor play
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Tested whether less caregiver interaction and sleep statistically account for part of the screen link; outdoor activity did not.

rows.title: Chen et al. (2021): screen time and autistic-like behaviors in Chinese preschoolers
rows.short_title: Chen et al. 2021: screen time and autistic-like behaviors
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Earlier first exposure, longer daily time and more years of screens each went with autistic-like behaviors on a parent checklist.

rows.title: Sadeghi et al. (2021): a parent-child interaction program combined with less screen time
rows.short_title: Sadeghi 2021: parent-child interaction and screen reduction
rows.type: Small intervention study (design and control condition [VERIFY])
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Reported lower autism-trait scores and EEG changes after a parent-child program plus screen reduction; the two cannot be separated.

rows.title: Kushima et al. (2022): screen time at age 1 and autism by age 3 in the Japan Environment and Children's Study
rows.short_title: Kushima 2022: screen time at 1 and autism at 3 (Japan)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: In boys but not girls, longer screen time at age 1 was associated with autism by age 3; the pattern was not a clean dose-response.

rows.title: Pouretemad et al. (2022): "Post-Digital Nannying Autism Syndrome" compared with autism
rows.short_title: Pouretemad 2022: the proposed 'PDNAS' label
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Compared 15 heavily screen-exposed children with sub-threshold autistic traits to 15 autistic and 15 non-autistic children.

rows.title: Heffler, Frome and Gullo (2022): a case report of two young children
rows.short_title: Heffler 2022: case report of two young children
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Two autistic children's developmental paths changed as screen time was cut and replaced with social time, then raised, then cut again.

rows.title: Moktan et al. (2022): screen time and autism-like signs during the COVID-19 pandemic in Nepal
rows.short_title: Moktan 2022: pandemic screen time and autism-like signs
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Describes more children presenting with autism-like signs alongside more screen time during lockdowns; no controls.

rows.title: Spitzer (2023): "Babys und Bildschirme: Realer oder virtueller Autismus?"
rows.short_title: Spitzer 2023: 'Real or virtual autism?' (German review)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Reviews Harlé's case compilation and the rise in recorded autism prevalence, including broader diagnostic concepts and awareness. Its conclusion on causation is unconfirmed.

rows.title: Sadeghi et al. (2023): screen time and autism "severity" scores in 68 autistic toddlers
rows.short_title: Sadeghi 2023: screen time and autism "severity" scores in toddlers
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Among autistic toddlers, more screen time appeared to go with higher "severity" scores (the study's term for how many autistic traits were rated).

rows.title: Islamabad, Pakistan (2023): children re-assessed after screen limits and speech and behavior support
rows.short_title: Pakistan 2023: re-assessment after screen limits and support
rows.type: Prospective descriptive case series (no control group)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: After 10 to 12 months of speech and behavior support plus screen limits, 24 of 30 children scored outside the autism range on repeat testing; no control group.

rows.title: Garg et al. (2024): a narrative review that presents "virtual autism" as established
rows.short_title: Garg et al. 2024: a review treating the term as established
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Describes the term as signs from heavy device use that are 'often reversible' and recommends limits; does not weigh reverse causation.

rows.title: Hill, Gangi and Miller (2024): screen time at 18 months and later autism and ADHD outcomes
rows.short_title: Hill et al. 2024: toddler screen time and later outcomes
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Toddlers later identified with autism or ADHD concerns had more screen time at 18 months; direction cannot be told.

rows.title: Al Moussawi, Bendak and Ziab (2024): early screen exposure in Lebanese children aged 0 to 3
rows.short_title: Al Moussawi 2024: early screens and CARS scores (Lebanon)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Among 73 children, those first exposed at 0 to 6 months had the highest average behavior and autism-rating scores.

rows.title: Heffler et al. (2024): early TV and video exposure and sensory processing
rows.short_title: Heffler 2024: early TV and sensory processing
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Early TV/video exposure was associated with atypical sensory-processing scores at about 33 months; not an autism study.

rows.title: Yuan et al. (2024 online): a systematic review of screen time and autism
rows.short_title: Yuan et al.: systematic review of screen time and autism
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Reports an association between preschool screen exposure and autism, larger with longer exposure; publication-bias handling unknown.

rows.title: "Decoding virtual autism" (2025 preprint)
rows.short_title: A 2025 preprint on 'decoding virtual autism'
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: A preprint describing 'so-called virtual autism'; not peer reviewed and not usable as evidence.

rows.title: Patterns of early screen exposure in autistic children (Tunisia, 2025)
rows.short_title: Tunisia 2025: early screen patterns in autistic toddlers
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Autistic toddlers started TV earlier and watched far more, mostly alone and often repetitive content; the viewing style itself may reflect autism.

rows.title: Sundarimaa et al. (2025): screen time and autism screening scores in Singapore toddlers
rows.short_title: Sundarimaa 2025: screen time and M-CHAT in Singapore
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Toddlers above the average 1.31 h/day had about 24% higher odds of a positive autism screen, strongest for social-communication items.

rows.title: Liu et al. (2025): a meta-analysis of screen exposure and autism in children
rows.short_title: Liu et al. 2025: meta-analysis of 10 screen-autism studies
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Autistic children had more screen exposure than controls across 10 studies; a group difference cannot show which came first.

rows.title: Georgia (2026): screen time and autism-like behavior in 1,834 toddlers
rows.short_title: Georgia 2026: screen time and autism screening (n=1,834)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Higher average daily screen time went with higher M-CHAT-R/F scores among 1,834 toddlers.

rows.title: Rangaraj et al. (2026): a small case-control study, and a lesson in unstable numbers
rows.short_title: Rangaraj 2026: a small case-control study with unstable odds
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: 43 vs. 43 children; adjusted odds ratios of 32 and 56 with enormous confidence intervals, a sign of sparse data.

rows.title: Başaran: "Sanal otizm" as a developmental risk (Turkish review)
rows.short_title: Başaran: 'sanal otizm' as a developmental risk (Turkish)
rows.stance_label: Reports or argues for a link
rows.one_line: Presents the term (credited to Zamfir) as a developmental risk and recommends fewer early screens and more parent-child interaction.

rows.title: Alrahili et al. (2021): screen time and social-communication scores in Saudi 4-to-6-year-olds
rows.short_title: Alrahili 2021: screen time and social-communication scores
rows.stance_label: Result not yet confirmed
rows.one_line: Surveyed screen time and social-communication scores in children aged 4 to 6; the result is unconfirmed.

rows.title: "Role of Genetic Risk in the Association Between Screen Time and Child Development" (2024 letter and reply)
rows.short_title: 2024 letter: genetic risk, screen time and development
rows.stance_label: Result not yet confirmed
rows.one_line: Correspondence on whether genetic likelihood explains part of the screen time-development link; content and authorship unconfirmed.

rows.title: "Are screens stealing childhood?" (2025): a case-control study we could not read
rows.short_title: 'Are screens stealing childhood?' (2025 case-control)
rows.stance_label: Result not yet confirmed
rows.one_line: 240 children aged 1 to 4 (120 with autism-like signs, 120 without); results not seen.

rows.title: "Screen Use and Children's Language Development From Ages 5 to 7 Years" (title only)
rows.short_title: Screen use and language from 5 to 7 (title only)
rows.stance_label: Result not yet confirmed
rows.one_line: Title only; findings unknown.

rows.title: American Academy of Pediatrics (2016): "Media and Young Minds"
rows.short_title: AAP 2016: 'Media and Young Minds' (earlier guidance)
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: 2016 AAP advice for under-5s: avoid screens other than video chat under 18 months; co-view high-quality content; about 1 hour a day at 2 to 5 [VERIFY].

rows.title: Madigan et al. (2019): screen time and children's scores on a developmental screening test
rows.short_title: Madigan 2019: screen time and developmental screening scores
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: More screen time at 2 and 3 was associated with slightly lower developmental screening scores a year or two later [VERIFY].

rows.title: World Health Organization (2019): guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5
rows.short_title: WHO 2019: activity, sitting and sleep for under-5s
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: No screen time for infants under 1; no more than 1 hour a day for ages 2 to 4; 180 minutes of varied physical activity a day for ages 1 to 4.

rows.title: Madigan et al. (2020): screen use and children's language skills
rows.short_title: Madigan 2020: screen use and language, a meta-analysis
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: More screen time and background TV went with weaker language; educational content and co-viewing went with stronger language.

rows.title: Mohamed et al. (2023): a digital-detox program for middle-school students
rows.short_title: Mohamed et al. 2023: a school digital-detox program
rows.type: Pre/post study without a control group
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: Among 105 Egyptian middle-schoolers, self-reported screen 'addiction' levels were lower after a detox program; no control group.

rows.title: Takahashi I et al. (2023): screen time at age 1 and communication and problem-solving delays at 2 and 4
rows.short_title: Takahashi I 2023: screen time at 1 and later delays
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: More screen time at 1 went with higher odds of communication and problem-solving delays at 2 and 4, in a dose-response pattern.

rows.title: Yamamoto et al. (2023): screen time and developmental scores at ages 1 to 3, tested in both directions
rows.short_title: Yamamoto 2023: TV/DVD time and development, both directions
rows.type: Cohort (national birth cohort; designed to test direction)
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: More TV/DVD at 1 and 2 went with lower scores a year later; lower scores went with more later viewing where mothers had psychological distress.

rows.title: Brushe et al. (2024): screen time and parent-child talk from 12 to 36 months
rows.short_title: Brushe 2024: screen time and parent-child talk
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: At 36 months, more screen time was associated with 1,139 fewer adult words, 843 fewer child vocalizations and 194 fewer conversational turns a day.

rows.title: Mallawaarachchi et al. (2024): early childhood screen-use contexts and outcomes
rows.short_title: Mallawaarachchi 2024: how under-5s use screens
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: Background TV, more program viewing and caregiver screen use went with poorer outcomes; co-use went with better thinking skills.

rows.title: Pliska et al. (2025): what parents of autistic children think about media
rows.short_title: Pliska et al. 2025: parents' views on media and autism
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: Parents of autistic children worried more about media effects yet saw more daily media time as acceptable.

rows.title: Vanderloo et al. (2025): screen time among children and youth with disabilities
rows.short_title: Vanderloo 2025: screen time in children with disabilities
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: Autistic children and youth had the highest reported screen time (0.5 to 7.27 h/day across studies); says nothing about cause.

rows.title: American Academy of Pediatrics (2026): "Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents" policy statement
rows.short_title: AAP 2026: 'Digital Ecosystems' policy statement
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: Frames children's media as 'digital ecosystems' and reportedly replaces earlier AAP media guidance; early-childhood specifics unconfirmed.

rows.title: American Academy of Pediatrics (2026): "Digital Ecosystems" technical report
rows.short_title: AAP 2026: 'Digital Ecosystems' technical report
rows.stance_label: Background (not a test of the screens-autism question)
rows.one_line: The evidence base for the 2026 AAP statement; its early-childhood conclusions are unknown to us.
